source.title: Privacy for free in the overparameterized regime

page_placements.theme: Privacy perturbations change sample and stopping requirements

record.tranche_reason: The study tests model-size and training-time error patterns in private training and random-feature regression, and reports that DP-GD can lack the interpolation peak seen with non-private GD.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the study's own sweeps over model size, sample size, and training iterations. The theoretical privacy bound is not a result about double descent. Mentioned double-descent results from cited work are not rows. Numerical values in the plots are not stated in the text, so plotted values are recorded as figure only.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps model size in its own random-features experiment and reports a double-descent curve with a peak at p = n under non-private GD. Under performance-tuned DP-GD (noise plus early stopping) there is no interpolation peak. The MNIST width sweep under DP-GD likewise shows no peak. This is a new setting (private training) with direct results on the size-wise curve. T3 fits better than T5: the authors do not argue that any version is wrong; their aim is a privacy-utility bound.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The main conclusion is theoretical: in sufficiently overparameterized random-features models, DP-GD has vanishing excess population risk even when ε = o(1) ('privacy for free'), so overparameterization is not at odds with private learning. The experiments support this. The ridge-like regularization explanation for the missing peak is offered as an interpretation, not tested.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates differentially private gradient descent and compares it with non-private GD; its experiments do not reproduce the original double-descent method as a general study of model-size, epoch, and sample-size axes.
record.method_sensitivity: The size-sweep outcome differs between non-private GD, which shows double descent in random features, and DP-GD, which steadily improves and plateaus. The reported optimal training time decreases with p; curves collapse under the ηTp/d rescaling.

fits_no_version.finding: In a fixed, strongly overparameterized MNIST network, DP-GD accuracy rises with n toward the non-private baseline once GD saturates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Surplus samples beyond what non-private learning needs are used to pay for privacy.

fits_no_version.finding: The optimal DP-GD stopping time decreases with p; loss curves collapse when plotted against ηTp/d.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal early-stopping time in DP-GD for random features scales as d/p.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
record.problems: The empirical curves are presented as plots without numerical values or reported uncertainty. Training-time curves are not described in enough textual detail to determine their shape. The MNIST model-size result is for DP-GD, and the random-features experiment tests only one synthetic setting.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant reported results were left out. Figure 3's clipping-and-iteration hyperparameter grid and Figure 4's grid search report utility across hyperparameters, but do not separately measure a claim version's named curve or mechanism.

untested.parts: Non-private (standard) training of deep networks across width. Only DP-GD is swept on MNIST.
Entirely. The T sweeps confound training time with privacy noise magnitude.
Entirely. The sample sweep uses a fixed model far above the interpolation threshold.
Label-noise dependence, multiple or triple descent, and conventional optimally tuned ridge (only discussed by analogy).

record.verdict_notes: The MNIST interpolation threshold (about n × classes ≈ 5×10^5 parameters) lies inside the swept range, yet DP-GD never interpolates, so the absence of a peak is expected under regularized training. That is why R1 is treated as limits_scope rather than challenges for V1. The random-features task has no explicit label noise (y = sign(u⊤x)). All values are figure-only.

versions.untested_parts: The model-size sweep is for DP-trained networks, not a general test of non-private deep networks across training methods.
The text reports error as training iterations vary and gives the minimizing iteration's scaling, but does not describe whether the error follows a fall-rise-fall shape.
The sample-size sweep is in a fixed, strongly overparameterized setting; it does not test increasing data near the interpolation threshold.
The study's own non-private double-descent result is for random features, not a sweep across multiple model classes or a test of whether the curve subsumes the classical U-shaped curve generally.
The study tests a scaling for optimal training time with model size, but not a single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.

The results bear on the absence of an interpolation peak under DP-GD and the authors' regularization interpretation. They do not test label-noise dependence, multiple or triple descent, or optimally tuned conventional regularization.
The study does not recount complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether this changes the curve to an ordinary U shape.

rows.note: The authors say DP-GD test loss steadily improves with p and plateaus near the corresponding GD loss, without the interpolation peak. They interpret the missing peak as a regularizing effect resembling ridge; this is not a test of conventional regularization.
rows.check: For V4 the state is partial: test loss keeps improving past p = n and plateaus near the GD loss, so the 'bigger is better' part holds, but there is no peak. For V6 the state should be observed: the peak is absent under performance-tuned DP-GD, which the authors liken to a ridge penalty. This is noise plus early stopping, not conventionally tuned ridge.

rows.subject: Random features model
rows.operation_detail: Varied training iterations T and plotted DP-GD test loss, including a rescaling of the iteration axis.

rows.note: The authors state that the minimizing T decreases with p and that the curves collapse when the axis is rescaled by ηTp/d. They do not describe the test-loss curve's shape over training time.
rows.check: This is not a measure of epoch-wise double descent. At fixed ε, the injected noise scales with ηT, so the loss-versus-T curve mixes training time with noise level. The shape is also not described. Should not link to V2.
